title: JSON: Save and Load Python Data as Text Anyone Can Read
excerpt: Turn dictionaries and lists into JSON text and back with json.dumps and json.loads, and save them to files with dump and load.

headings.text: JSON Text Back to Python Data
Save to a File and Load It Back
When the Text Is Not Valid JSON

html:
Your program has built a dictionary full of useful data. The program ends, and the data vanishes. Or you need to send that data to another program, perhaps written in a completely different language. You need a way to turn Python data into plain text, and back again.

JSON is a simple text format for data that almost every language understands, and Python's built-in json module converts between JSON text and Python dictionaries and lists. It is the format behind most web APIs (the ways programs talk to each other over the internet) and many configuration files.

Python Data to JSON Text

The function json.dumps() takes Python data and returns a string of JSON. (The "s" stands for string.) Here person is a dictionary: labelled values written inside {}.

import json

person = {
    "name": "Asha",
    "age": 31,
    "skills": ["python", "sql"],
    "active": True,
    "manager": None,
}

text = json.dumps(person)

print(text)
print(type(text))
{"name": "Asha", "age": 31, "skills": ["python", "sql"], "active": true, "manager": null}
<class 'str'>

The result looks very much like the Python dictionary, with two differences you may have spotted. Why are true and null written in lowercase? Because JSON has its own spelling: Python's True becomes true and None becomes null. Also, JSON text always uses double quotes.

JSON Text Back to Python Data

The reverse function is json.loads(), which reads a JSON string and rebuilds the Python data:

data = json.loads(text)

print(data["skills"][1])
print(type(data))
print(data == person)
sql
<class 'dict'>
True

You get a normal dictionary back, so you can index into it as usual, and it is equal to the one you started with.

Make It Readable

By default dumps() puts everything on one line. Add indent to spread it out for human eyes, and sort_keys to order the keys alphabetically:

print(json.dumps(person, indent=2, sort_keys=True))
{
  "active": true,
  "age": 31,
  "manager": null,
  "name": "Asha",
  "skills": [
    "python",
    "sql"
  ]
}

Save to a File and Load It Back

To write straight to a file, use json.dump() without the "s", passing the file object as the second argument. Why are there two pairs of functions? One pair works with text held in your program, the other works with files on disk. The with statement opens the file and closes it again when the block ends; the "w" means "open for writing", and the .read() at the end returns the whole file as text:

with open("person.json", "w") as file:
    json.dump(person, file, indent=2)

with open("person.json") as file:
    loaded = json.load(file)

print(loaded == person)
with open("person.json") as file:
    print(file.read())
True
{
  "name": "Asha",
  "age": 31,
  "skills": [
    "python",
    "sql"
  ],
  "active": true,
  "manager": null
}

So there are two pairs to remember. dumps and loads work with strings; dump and load work with files. Because the file is plain text, you can open person.json in any editor, send it to a colleague, or read it from a program written in another language. That portability is the main reason JSON is used for settings files and web APIs.

What JSON Cannot Keep Exactly

JSON is simpler than Python, so a few things change on the way through. Will you get back exactly what you saved? Not always:

print(json.dumps((1, 2)))
print(json.loads(json.dumps((1, 2))))
print(json.dumps({1: "a"}))
[1, 2]
[1, 2]
{"1": "a"}

A tuple (a fixed group of values, like (1, 2)) becomes a list, because JSON only has lists. And a dictionary key that is a number becomes text, because JSON keys must be strings. Some Python values cannot be stored at all:

json.dumps({"tags": {"a", "b"}})
TypeError: Object of type set is not JSON serializable

JSON has no set type (a set is a collection with no duplicates, like {"a", "b"}), so Python raises a TypeError instead of guessing; "not JSON serializable" means it cannot be written out as JSON text. Convert such values yourself first, for example with list().

When the Text Is Not Valid JSON

JSON is strict. Python dictionaries allow single quotes, but JSON does not:

json.loads("{'name': 'Asha'}")
JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)

The error message points to where the problem starts. When you read JSON from an outside source, remember that it can be invalid, and be ready for an error like this one; programs usually guard against it with a try and except block, which catches the error and lets you respond.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonJson.ipynb.

Summary

  • json.dumps(data) turns Python data into a JSON string; json.loads(text) turns it back.
  • json.dump(data, file) and json.load(file) do the same with files.
  • Python's True, False and None become true, false and null in JSON.
  • indent=2 and sort_keys=True make the output readable.
  • Tuples come back as lists and number keys come back as text; sets cannot be stored.
  • Invalid JSON, such as single-quoted strings, raises a JSONDecodeError.
